meta.title: The Cones That Wait for Fire
meta.theme: pine trees whose cones open only in the heat of a forest fire, so that the fire becomes the start of the next forest
meta.learning_objective: close a short process description on what the process means for the thing described, not on a moral for all of nature

source.usage_note: Original composition in CAT register for CAT OS. A general description of fire-dependent seed release in some pines; no specific text adapted. Personal study only.

meta.reviewer_notes: Three steps of a process: sealed cones, resin that melts in fire, seeds on cleared ground. The conclusion has to name what the steps add up to for these trees: the fire is how they start again.

quality.adversarial_review: The live rival is the line that nature wastes nothing. It is warm, it feels like a lesson, and it is in the spirit of the paragraph; but it leaves these pines behind for all of nature and claims that every disaster serves a purpose, which three sentences about one kind of tree cannot support. The fire-fighting option reverses the paragraph's view of fire, and the restatement repeats the first two sentences.

sentences: Some pine trees keep their cones shut tight for years, sealed with a hard resin.
The resin melts only in great heat, such as the heat of a forest fire.
Once the fire has passed, the cones open and drop their seeds onto ground that has been cleared of other plants and covered in fresh ash.

question.stem: Which of the following sentences best completes the paragraph?

options.A: This is why forest fires must be put out quickly, before they can reach the pines and destroy them.
options.B: So the cones of these pines stay closed until a fire comes along that is hot enough to melt them open.
options.C: For these trees, the fire that ends the old forest is also the way the new forest begins.
options.D: Nature wastes nothing, and in the end every disaster turns out to serve some purpose.

explanation.what_the_gap_needs: The paragraph describes three steps: cones sealed shut, resin that melts only in fire, seeds dropped on cleared ground after the fire. A closing sentence should say what these steps mean for the trees, and it should keep the paragraph's view of fire as part of the trees' life rather than only a danger to them.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option draws the conclusion the three steps point to: for these pines the fire is not only an ending but also the way a new forest starts. It stays with 'these trees' and keeps the paragraph's calm, describing tone.

distractors.why_wrong: The paragraph shows that these pines depend on fire to release their seeds; telling us fires must be stopped before they reach the pines turns that view upside down.
distractors.seductive_element: Putting out forest fires sounds sensible and responsible, and readers bring that view with them.

distractors.why_wrong: The first two sentences have already said the cones stay sealed until fire melts the resin; repeating it adds nothing and ignores what happens after the fire.
distractors.seductive_element: It sounds like a careful summary and uses the paragraph's own words.

distractors.why_wrong: It jumps from one kind of pine to all of nature and claims every disaster serves a purpose, which is far more than three sentences about one tree can support.
distractors.seductive_element: It is quotable and hopeful, and broad lessons often feel like the natural way to end.

explanation.method: For a paragraph that describes a process, ask what the process adds up to for the thing being described. Keep the ending at the same size as the paragraph: one kind of tree, not all of nature.

mentor.challenge: Three steps, from sealed cone to seed in the ash. Say what they add up to for these trees, and no more.
mentor.takeaway: A conclusion stays the size of the paragraph; a lesson for all of nature is bigger than three sentences can carry.
